blocks.text: This is a localized infection of the hair follicle on the outer one-third of the external auditory canal. It is caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Ear pain that is severe and disproportional to the visible lesion
Localized swelling on the external auditory canal
There may be a purulent discharge if the swelling ruptures
Aural toilet if there is otorrhea (ear suctioning under direct vision).
Aural toilet using a clean dry cotton cloth while at home.
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching
Antibiotics are reserved for cases with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, cellulitis) or microbiologically confirmed resistant infections. Routine use is discouraged to prevent antimicrobial resistance

runs.text: Routine use is discouraged to prevent antimicrobial resistance

blocks.text: This is an inflammation of the entire external auditory canal. It can be caused by bacteria, fungus or both.
Itchy, dry and scaly ear canal and painful ear
There may be a water or purulent discharge, debris and reduced hearing
Pain may become extreme when the ear canal becomes completely occluded with edematous skin and debris.
Aural toilet at least once a week (ear suctioning under direct vision using microscope or endoscope).
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching.
Topical Antibiotics: Preferred over systemic antibiotics to reduce resistance risk. Systemic antibiotics are not recommended unless there is evidence of cellulitis or systemic infection

runs.text: there is evidence of cellulitis or systemic infection

blocks.text: C: Topical cream (combination: Gentamicin or Neomycin + corticosteroid [Clobetasol/Betamethasone/Beclometasone] + antifungal [Miconazole/Clotrimazole])
Apply pea-sized amount in external auditory

This is a life-threatening invasive infection that affects the external auditory canal leading to skull base osteomyelitis. It is common to elderly diabetic patients and other immunosuppressive conditions. Most common causative organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa followed by Aspergillus. Controlling the underlying cause of immunosuppression is of paramount importance.

blocks.text: Nocturnal exquisite ear pain, discharge, fullness and hearing impairment.
May present with facial nerve paralysis or other cranial nerves palsy.
Oedema of the external auditory canal with or without presence of granulation tissues at the junction between the bony and cartilaginous parts of the inferior portion of external auditory canal
Aural toilet at least three sessions per week (ear suctioning under direct vision using microscope or endoscope) until disease is controlled.
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching
Culture and sensitivity of discharge and tissue.
Glycosylated hemoglobin HbA1c / Fasting blood glucose
Antibiotics: Systemic antibiotics are essential due to the severity and osteomyelitis risk. Treatment should be guided by culture and sensitivity result.
4 weeks, then de- escalate according to M/C/S

Note: Necrotizing otitis externa is an emergency therefore treatment should be vigorous including the treatment of underlaying immunodeficiency. Consider referral to tertiary facility for specialized care.

blocks.text: This is a viral infection of external, middle and inner ear caused by reactivation of Varicella Zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion.
Instruct the patient to keep the ear dry and avoiding scratching
Note: If there is involvement of the eyelid or eye refer to an ophthalmologist for review.
This is an infection of the pre-auricular sinus tract. May present with pre-auricular abscesses. Most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
Ear pain, sinus discharge, Pre-auricular Swelling, Fever, headache.
Antibiotics: Antibiotics are indicated only for active infection with abscess or cellulitis. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended
Incision and drainage of the abscess
Excision of the sinus tract two to three weeks after incision and drainage i.e., when the sinus tract is dry.
